vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room of his design studio, surrounded by swatches of silk and mood boards for next season's collection. At fifty-five, he's built a respected career, known for his meticulous attention to detail and his ability to sense what clients want before they articulate it. But lately, the studio feels like a place where he's performing competence rather than inhabiting it.

His childhood was spent in a small apartment with his mother and her boyfriend, Derek. Derek had a particular way of correcting Marcus—sudden, physical, unpredictable. A spilled glass of juice. A wrong answer to a question asked in anger. Marcus learned early to read the micro-expressions on Derek's face, the slight tension in his shoulders, the way his voice would drop before it escalated. By age twelve, Marcus could sense danger the way other children sensed hunger.

The hypervigilance never really left. Even now, when a client raises their voice in frustration about a design revision, Marcus feels his chest tighten. His hands move instinctively to protect his ribs—a gesture so automatic he barely notices it anymore. He's gotten good at disguising these moments, attributing his sudden silence to creative contemplation. But his assistant noticed last week when a delivery person knocked loudly on the studio door. Marcus flinched so visibly that she asked if he was alright. He said he was tired. That was easier than the truth.

Sleep has become complicated. Marcus lies awake most nights, his mind cataloging the day for threats he might have missed. Did his business partner seem frustrated? Was there an edge to the client's email? Around 3 a.m., he often finds himself in his home office, sketching designs that will never be made, his mind unable to settle into the rest his body desperately needs. When he does sleep, the dreams come—fragments of Derek's face, the sound of a belt being unbuckled, the feeling of being trapped in a space too small to escape.

His ex-wife used to tell him he was "emotionally unavailable," that he retreated into his work whenever things got difficult. She wasn't wrong. The studio became his refuge, a place where he could control every variable. Fabrics behave predictably. Seams can be ripped out and redone. People cannot. His divorce finalized three years ago, and he hasn't attempted another relationship since. The thought of someone getting close enough to see the damage underneath exhausts him.

What troubles Marcus most is the way shame has woven itself into his narrative. He's a successful man—he shouldn't be this afraid. A loud noise shouldn't send him into a state of vigilance that lasts for hours. He shouldn't avoid certain neighborhoods because they remind him of the apartment complex where he grew up. He shouldn't have panic attacks in the middle of important client meetings, attributing them to sudden migraines so he can excuse himself and sit in his car until his heart stops racing.

He's started avoiding his own studio after hours, unable to tolerate the silence that used to comfort him. The isolation that once felt like safety now feels like a prison of his own making. He tells himself he's simply getting older, that this is what fifty-five looks like. But somewhere beneath the carefully constructed professional persona, Marcus knows something else is happening—that the cost of survival has become unsustainable, and that the boy who learned to read danger in a small apartment is still running.
